newsitem.title: UK: Princess Diana pleads for ban on landmines.
newsitem.headline: Princess Diana pleads for ban on landmines.

text.p: Princess Diana on Wednesday made an impassioned plea for the world to ban landmines and said more should be done to help innocent victims.
"I think we owe it," said Diana who launched her anti-landmine campaign with a high-profile visit to Angola in January and now plans to visit Bosnia this week.
She won wholehearted support as well as security backing for her Bosnia trip from Foreign Secretary Robin Cook who said: "I have nothing but admiration for Princess Diana's crusade."
Diana, writing in the Mirror tabloid, said "The world is too little aware of the waste of life, limb and land which anti-personnel mines are causing some of the poorest people on earth."
She said that one in every 334 of the population in Angola is an amputee -- the highest rate in the world.

The princess has sought since her 1996 divorce from heir-to-the-throne Prince Charles to become a "queen of hearts" roving ambassador for Britain, espousing such causes as AIDS research and the landmine campaign.

Her Bosnia visit coincided with a flurry of political and diplomatic pressure on the country's factions to hand over war crime suspects and force a fair division of diplomatic posts by its ethnically split government.

The foreign office on Tuesday gave the princess the security go-ahead for the visit and Cook, also writing in The Mirror, said: "I publicly support her trip to Bosnia, a country littered with six million mines."
"If her visit to Bosnia is as successful as her trip to Angola, she will deserve thanks, not brickbats," he wrote.
Some British parliamentarians have accused Diana of meddling in international affairs but she insisted on Wednesday: "I am not a political figure. My interests are humanitarian."
Piling on the diplomatic pressure for a total ban, she said: "How can countries which manufacture and trade in these weapons square their conscience with such human devastation."
Complaining that "the evil that men do lives after them," she said 110 million mines are still lurking somewhere in the world and one third are found in Africa.
"I would like to see more done for those living in this no man's land which lies between the wrongs of yesterday and the urgent needs of today," she said.

Diana, seeking to stir the international conscience, said: "The world, with its many other preoccupations, remains largely unmoved by a death toll of something like 800 people every month -- many of them women and children."
